etymology: English surname; the Southern Presbyterian theologian James Henley Thornwell (1812–1862) of South Carolina.
biblical_def: James Henley Thornwell was the foremost Southern Presbyterian theologian of the antebellum period, a defender of strict Presbyterian church order, of the spirituality of the church, and of the regulative principle of worship. He held the Westminster standards with a rigor few of his generation matched, insisted that the church is a spiritual body whose charter is Scripture alone and whose officers may bind the conscience only where the Word binds it, and pressed the parity of elders and the jure divino character of Presbyterian government. His lectures on theology, gathered after his death, are a monument of Reformed scholastic precision. Yet Thornwell is a sobering case of how a faithful confessionalist may be blinded on a matter of justice: he defended chattel slavery as compatible with Scripture and opposed abolition, and in this he sinned against the plain word that condemns the man-stealer. The dictionary honors his churchmanship, his defense of the church’s spiritual independence, and his confessional fidelity, while naming his apology for slavery as a grievous error against the law of God, which forbids stealing a man and selling him (Exo 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10). His life proves that orthodoxy on the decree does not guarantee obedience on the second table, and that a man may see the throne of God clearly and yet not love his neighbor as himself.
webster_summary: Southern Presbyterian theologian (1812–1862); rigorous confessionalist and defender of the church’s spirituality, but a defender of slavery, which Scripture condemns.

corruption_summary: Thornwell’s memory is claimed both by those who would erase him for his sin and by those who would excuse his defense of slavery; both miss the biblical verdict.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions press on Thornwell’s legacy. The first would erase him entirely, treating his sin on slavery as the whole of the man and consigning his confessional labors to oblivion. This is not the way of Scripture, which records the sins of David and Solomon without erasing the psalms or the proverbs. The second corruption excuses or minimizes his defense of chattel slavery, treating it as a regrettable cultural blind spot rather than a sin against the law of God. The dictionary refuses both: it names the sin as sin, by its biblical name of man-stealing (Exo 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10), and it receives what was faithful in his churchmanship as faithful.

Thornwell stands as a warning against the assumption that doctrinal precision sanctifies the whole man. He saw the decree of God with rare clarity and yet failed to love his neighbor as himself in the most consequential matter of his age. The lesson is the one Paul presses: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1 Cor 8:1). A theology that does not bend the proud heart to do justly and love mercy (Mic 6:8) has not yet done its saving work. The remedy is not to abandon confessional rigor but to subject it, and the whole man, to the searching of the same Word.

etymology: Modern personal name; the Reformed Baptist preacher and author Voddie Baucham (b. 1969).
biblical_def: Voddie Baucham is a contemporary Reformed Baptist pastor, author, and apologist, known for his expository preaching, his defense of biblical patriarchy and family discipleship, his confessional Calvinism, and his warning against the worldly ideologies that have entered the evangelical church. Converted from a Buddhist-influenced upbringing, he came to embrace the doctrines of grace and the 1689 Baptist confession, and has labored to call the church back to Scripture as the sufficient and authoritative rule. His book on the cultural captivity of the church to critical theory argued, from the Reformed conviction that the gospel and not social ideology reconciles men, that the church must not exchange the biblical anthropology of one blood in Adam and one body in Christ for the oppressor-oppressed grid of the world. He has stressed the duty of fathers to disciple their households, the centrality of the local church, and the gospel as the only power unto salvation. As with every living teacher, the dictionary commends him not as an authority above Scripture but as a faithful witness in his generation, to be heard as the Bereans heard Paul, searching the Scriptures daily whether these things are so (Acts 17:11).
webster_summary: Contemporary Reformed Baptist preacher and author (b. 1969); confessional Calvinist, advocate of family discipleship, and critic of worldly ideology in the church.
webster_full: BAUCHAM, VODDIE, contemporary Reformed Baptist pastor and apologist, b. 1969.

Heard as a faithful witness, not as an authority above Scripture (Acts 17:11).

Eph 6:4

corruption_summary: His name is invoked both by partisans who would make him a culture-war mascot and by critics who dismiss confessional Calvinism as mere reaction; both miss the man and the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to resist is the reduction of a living preacher to a political symbol. Partisans on one side make Baucham a mascot of the culture war; critics on the other dismiss his confessional convictions as mere reaction. Both flatten a minister of the Word into a token in a quarrel that is not the church’s true battle. The dictionary’s interest is narrower and higher: does his teaching agree with Scripture? Where it calls the church to the sufficiency of the Word, to family discipleship, and to the gospel as the only reconciling power, it agrees, and is commended on those grounds and no other.

A second danger is the temptation, common to admirers of any gifted teacher, to receive a man’s words as if they carried the authority of the Word itself. No living teacher is an oracle. The Bereans were commended not for crediting Paul on his office but for searching the Scriptures daily to test his preaching (Acts 17:11). Every contemporary voice, including the most faithful, is to be weighed in that same balance. The confession itself confesses that synods and councils may err, and that Scripture alone binds the conscience absolutely.

etymology: Personal name; the Presbyterian (PCA) pastor and author Timothy J. Keller (1950–2023).
biblical_def: Timothy Keller was a Presbyterian minister in the Presbyterian Church in America, founding pastor of Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan, and a widely read author who labored to commend the historic Christian faith to a skeptical, secular, urban culture. He held the Westminster standards, preached justification by faith alone and the grace of God in Christ, and pressed the application of the gospel against both the irreligion of the licentious and the self-righteousness of the moralist—his recurring theme that the gospel is neither religion nor irreligion but a third thing. His books on prayer, on suffering, on marriage, and on the reasons for God reached many outside the church and within it. The dictionary honors his clear preaching of grace and his gift for apologetic translation, while noting the cautions raised by Reformed brethren: that his cultural winsomeness at times softened the harder edges of biblical confrontation, and that his approach to questions of creation and to engagement with the city drew confessional scrutiny. As with every teacher, his writings are to be received under the Word and tested by it, holding fast that which is good (1 Thess 5:21).
webster_summary: PCA pastor and author (1950–2023); preached justification by grace to a secular culture; honored for gospel clarity, with Reformed cautions on cultural accommodation.
webster_full: KELLER, TIMOTHY J., Presbyterian (PCA) pastor and author, 1950–2023.
Founding pastor of Redeemer Presbyterian Church, New York City.
Pressed the gospel as a third thing over against both irreligion and moralism.
Widely read author on prayer, suffering, marriage, and the reasons for God.
Received under the Word; tested by it, holding fast that which is good (1 Thess 5:21).
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Eph 2:8

corruption_summary: Keller is treated by some as beyond criticism and by others as a compromiser; the biblical course is to test his teaching by the Word and hold fast what is good.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to resist runs in two directions. Some admirers receive Keller’s every formulation as settled wisdom, declining to test it; some critics reduce his whole ministry to its weaker moments. Neither is the way of the Bereans. The dictionary commends his plain preaching of justification by grace and his skill in setting the gospel against both license and self-righteousness, and it notes, soberly and by name, the confessional cautions: that a winsome cultural posture can blunt the offense of the cross (1 Cor 1:23), and that engagement with the secular city must never trade away the antithesis between the wisdom of God and the wisdom of the world.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is discernment toward living teachers: prove all things, hold fast that which is good (1 Thess 5:21). A gifted minister may preach grace truly and still need to be weighed where his cultural method softens what Scripture sharpens. To honor what is faithful and to test what is doubtful is not ingratitude; it is the obedience the Word itself commands of every hearer.

etymology: English personal name; the evangelical statesman William Wilberforce (1759–1833), leader of the British abolition of the slave trade.
biblical_def: William Wilberforce was an English member of Parliament whose evangelical conversion turned his life toward two great objects, as he wrote: the suppression of the slave trade and the reformation of manners. Awakened to a living faith in Christ, he counted the costly labor of abolition as obedience to God, who has made of one blood all nations of men (Acts 17:26) and who hears the cry of the oppressed. For decades he pressed the cause against entrenched commercial interests, until in 1807 Parliament abolished the British slave trade, and on his deathbed in 1833 he learned that slavery itself would be abolished throughout the empire. He labored also for the moral renewal of England, for missions, and for the relief of the poor, holding that true faith bears fruit in works of mercy. His Practical View of real Christianity rebuked the nominal religion of his day and called for a vital, heart-changing faith. Wilberforce stands as a witness that the gospel, rightly held, arms the conscience against the great injustices of the age, and that the man who fears God will plead the cause of the poor and needy (Pro 31:8-9).
webster_summary: English evangelical statesman (1759–1833) who led the abolition of the British slave trade; a witness that living faith pleads the cause of the oppressed.
webster_full: WILBERFORCE, WILLIAM, English evangelical statesman, 1759–1833.
Member of Parliament; led the campaign against the British slave trade.
Abolition of the trade carried in 1807; of slavery itself in 1833 at his death.

A witness that the fear of God arms the conscience to plead for the oppressed (Pro 31:8-9).

Isa 1:17

corruption_summary: Wilberforce is claimed as a mere humanitarian shorn of his faith; in truth his abolition labor was the direct fruit of evangelical conversion.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to resist is the secular retelling that severs Wilberforce’s achievement from its root. He is often presented as a humanitarian reformer whose religion was incidental decoration on a fundamentally secular conscience. The record refuses this: his own account names his evangelical conversion as the spring of all that followed, and his Practical View argued that only a vital, heart-changing Christianity could sustain such labor. To strip the faith from the man is to misread both. The gospel did not hinder his justice; it was the very thing that armed it.

A subtler error treats abolition as the fruit of an autonomous moral progress that the church merely caught up to. Scripture tells the truth more plainly: the law had forbidden man-stealing from Sinai (Exo 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10), and the prophets had commanded the relief of the oppressed (Isa 1:17). Wilberforce did not invent a new morality; he obeyed an old one, against the commercial idols of his day. His life is therefore a rebuke not to faith but to the nominal religion that calls itself Christian and yet keeps silent before great wrong.

etymology: From southern + Presbyterian; the Reformed Presbyterian tradition of the American South, organized as the PCUS in 1861.
biblical_def: Southern Presbyterianism is the Reformed Presbyterian tradition of the American South, which took organized form in the Presbyterian Church in the United States (the old PCUS) at the division of 1861. Its theology was confessional and Westminsterian, marked by a high doctrine of the spirituality of the church—the conviction, pressed by Thornwell and Dabney, that the church is a spiritual body whose commission is the gospel and whose officers may not bind the conscience to political programs Scripture has not commanded. At its best the tradition produced rigorous systematic theology, devoted churchmen, and a love for the Westminster standards. Yet the same tradition is shadowed by its complicity in the defense of chattel slavery and, later, of racial segregation, sins that its doctrine of the church’s spirituality was too often used to shield rather than to rebuke. The dictionary receives the genuine theological gifts of Southern Presbyterianism—its confessionalism, its churchmanship, its labors in doctrine—while naming its racial sins as sins against the God who made of one blood all nations (Acts 17:26). The tradition is thus a mingled inheritance: faithful on the decree and the sacraments, gravely failing on the love of neighbor.
webster_summary: The Reformed Presbyterian tradition of the American South (PCUS, 1861); confessional and Westminsterian, but shadowed by its defense of slavery and segregation.
webster_full: SOUTHERN PRESBYTERIANISM, the Reformed Presbyterian tradition of the American South.
Organized as the Presbyterian Church in the United States (PCUS) in 1861.
Confessional and Westminsterian; high doctrine of the spirituality of the church.

Shadowed by complicity in slavery and segregation, sins against Acts 17:26.
scriptures: And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Gal 3:28

corruption_summary: The tradition is romanticized by some as purely faithful and dismissed by others as wholly corrupt; the biblical verdict honors its doctrine and names its racial sins.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions attend the memory of Southern Presbyterianism. The first romanticizes it, treating its confessional rigor as if it covered its racial sins, and invoking the spirituality of the church to silence rather than to sharpen the conscience. The second dismisses the tradition wholesale, as if a body that erred grievously on slavery could have given the church nothing of value. Scripture warrants neither. The Chronicler records mixed reigns as mixed; so the dictionary receives the doctrinal labors of this tradition and condemns its respect of persons (Jas 2:9) as transgression of the law.

The deeper lesson concerns the doctrine of the church’s spirituality itself, which is true and precious when it guards the church from being captured by party politics, but which becomes a cloak for sin when it is used to forbid the church from naming the oppression of image-bearers. The spirituality of the church was never meant to silence the prophets who cried, let judgment run down as waters (Amos 5:24). A right doctrine, abused to shield a sin, becomes a snare; the remedy is not to discard the doctrine but to recover its true and limited use under the whole counsel of God.

etymology: From New England + Puritan; the English Calvinist settlers of seventeenth-century Massachusetts and Connecticut.
biblical_def: The New England Puritans were the English Calvinist settlers who, fleeing the corruptions and persecutions of the Old World, planted in Massachusetts, Connecticut, and the neighboring colonies a society ordered, in their intention, by the Word of God. They held a covenantal theology, a congregational church order, the regulative principle of worship, and a vision of a community in covenant with God—a city upon a hill, as Winthrop preached, whose obedience or disobedience would be visible to all. They prized preaching, catechism, the Sabbath, learning (founding Harvard for a literate ministry), and the searching of the heart for the marks of saving grace. Their literature of practical divinity—the diaries, the sermons, the casuistry—remains among the richest in the English tongue. Yet their record is mingled: the genuine piety stood alongside grave failures, including the injustice done to the native peoples and the tragedy at Salem, where the fear of witchcraft overran the bounds of biblical justice. The dictionary honors the Puritan recovery of experiential, covenantal, Word-governed religion, while measuring the failures of the colonies by the same Scripture they professed, that the children of light might learn from both their fidelity and their sin.
webster_summary: The English Calvinist settlers of seventeenth-century New England; covenantal, congregational, Word-governed in intention, with rich piety and mingled failures.
webster_full: NEW ENGLAND PURITANS, English Calvinist settlers of seventeenth-century New England.

scriptures: Mat 5:14

corruption_summary: The Puritans are caricatured as joyless tyrants or idealized as flawless saints; both miss the mingled record of genuine piety and real sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern caricature of the Puritan—a joyless, repressive bigot—is a corruption born of ignorance and of a culture that resents any people who feared God and ordered life by His Word. The Puritans wrote tenderly of marriage, of beauty, of the affections rightly ordered toward God; their practical divinity is a treasury of pastoral wisdom on the inner life. To dismiss them as gloomy tyrants is to slander a people whom Scripture would call, in much, faithful, and to forfeit the riches of their experiential religion.

The opposite corruption idealizes the Puritan colonies as a flawless biblical commonwealth, passing over their real sins: the injustices done to the native peoples and the failure of justice at Salem, where the bounds the law itself sets upon evidence and witness were overrun. The dictionary does neither. It honors the Puritan recovery of covenantal, Word-governed, heart-searching religion (2 Cor 13:5), and it measures the colonies’ failures by the very Scripture they professed, that requires men to do justly and love mercy (Mic 6:8). The children of light are to learn from both.

etymology: From second + great awakening; the American revival movement of roughly 1790–1840.
biblical_def: The Second Great Awakening was a wave of religious revival that swept the American frontier and the established churches from roughly 1790 into the 1840s, marked by camp meetings, fervent preaching, and a great increase of professed conversions, voluntary societies, and missionary and reform labor. Genuine grace was at work in much of it: many were truly converted, churches were planted on the frontier, and the energies of awakened believers flowed into Bible societies, missions, and works of mercy. Yet the movement is a mixed inheritance, for alongside the true work ran a corrupting theology, most visibly in Charles Finney, who denied the Reformed doctrines of human inability and sovereign regeneration and taught that revival is not a miracle of God but the right use of means—the result of a properly worked-up excitement. This man-centered method, with its new measures, sowed seeds of the decisionism and emotional manipulation that have plagued American evangelicalism since. The dictionary distinguishes the true work of the Spirit, who quickens whom He will, from the Pelagianizing theology that learned to manufacture its counterfeit, and tests every awakening by its fruit and its doctrine, that the church may rejoice in the one and refuse the other.
webster_summary: American revival movement (c. 1790–1840); genuine grace mixed with the man-centered revivalism of Finney, whose new measures sowed decisionism.
webster_full: SECOND GREAT AWAKENING, American revival movement, c. 1790–1840.

Fueled Bible societies, missions, and works of reform and mercy.
Corrupted in part by Finney, who made revival a worked-up result of means.
His new measures sowed the decisionism that plagues evangelicalism since.

corruption_summary: The Awakening is idealized as a pure outpouring or dismissed as mere emotionalism; the truth distinguishes the real work of the Spirit from Finney’s man-centered counterfeit.
corruption_paragraphs: The corrupting theology of the Second Great Awakening is most sharply seen in Charles Finney, who taught that the new birth is not a sovereign work of God upon a dead and unable sinner but the natural result of rightly applied means—that revival could be produced by men as a crop is produced by farming. This is a denial of the plain word that men are born not of the will of man but of God (John 1:13), and that the wind of the Spirit blows where it lists (John 3:8). Finney’s new measures—the anxious bench, the protracted meeting engineered for effect—trained generations to mistake aroused emotion for regeneration.

Yet the answer to Finney’s error is not to dismiss the whole season as mere emotionalism, for God truly converted many and truly advanced His church through it. The dictionary therefore divides the spoil: it rejoices in the genuine work of the Spirit, who gave the increase (1 Cor 3:6), and it refuses the Pelagianizing method that learned to manufacture a counterfeit. Every awakening is to be tried by its doctrine and its fruit. Where men are truly humbled, brought to Christ, and made holy, God is at work; where excitement is engineered and inability denied, the work is of man, and will not stand.

etymology: From non- (not) + conform; the English Protestants who would not conform to the imposed worship and government of the established Church.
biblical_def: Nonconformity is the historic stance of those English Protestants—Puritans, Presbyterians, Independents, Baptists, and others—who, after the Act of Uniformity of 1662, would not conform to the imposed liturgy, ceremonies, and episcopal government of the established Church of England, and who therefore suffered ejection from their livings, fines, and imprisonment. The Great Ejection of 1662 cast out some two thousand faithful ministers in a single day. The nonconformist conscience rested on the regulative principle—that God alone is Lord of the conscience in worship, and that what He has not commanded in His worship is not lawfully imposed by men—and on the headship of Christ over His church against the encroachments of the magistrate. From this suffering people came Bunyan, writing from his Bedford prison, Owen and Baxter among the ejected, and the long tradition of English dissent. The dictionary honors nonconformity as a faithful refusal to add to the worship of God what He has not appointed, and as a witness that Christ, not the crown, is head of the church; it is the historic seedbed of confessional Baptist and Independent conviction, and a standing rebuke to every attempt to bind the conscience where Scripture has left it free.
webster_summary: The stance of English Protestants who refused the imposed worship and government of the established Church; rooted in the regulative principle and Christ’s headship.
webster_full: NONCONFORMITY, refusal to conform to the imposed worship of the established Church.

Rested on the regulative principle and the headship of Christ over His church.

corruption_summary: Nonconformity is dismissed as mere stubbornness or recast as generic anti-authority dissent; in truth it was conscience bound to the Word against unlawful imposition.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption recasts nonconformity as mere obstinacy, a refusal to keep the peace, as though the dissenters quarreled over trifles of ceremony. But the issue was never trifling: it was whether men may impose upon the worship of God what God has not commanded, and whether the crown or Christ is head of the church. To call such conscience stubbornness is to side with the persecutor against the persecuted, and to forget that we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

A subtler corruption baptizes the word nonconformist into the modern cult of generic dissent—rebellion against authority as such, conformity to nothing. This is the opposite of the historic stance. The nonconformists were the most scrupulously conscience-bound of men, refusing one authority precisely because they were bound to a higher one, the Word of God. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond this drift. The principle to recover is that the conscience is free under Scripture and bound by it, never a law unto itself, and that worship must be governed by what God has appointed, not by the commandments of men (Mat 15:9).
roots_summary: Non- + conform; the English Protestants who refused the imposed worship of the established Church, bound in conscience to the Word.
roots_lines: Nonconformity — refusal to conform to the established Church’s imposed worship.
The Great Ejection of 1662 cast out some two thousand ministers.
Rested on the regulative principle and the headship of Christ (Col 1:18).
Produced Bunyan, the ejected divines, and confessional dissent.
Obey God rather than men (Act 5:29) — conscience bound to the Word.
usage: The Act of Uniformity drove faithful ministers into nonconformity in 1662.
Nonconformity refused to add to God’s worship what He had not commanded.
Its dissent was conscience bound to Scripture, not rebellion against authority as such.

etymology: From Puritan + casuistry (the resolving of cases of conscience), Latin casus, a case.
biblical_def: Puritan casuistry is the Reformed art of resolving cases of conscience—the careful, pastoral application of Scripture to the particular questions, doubts, and temptations of the believing soul. Over against the Roman casuistry that had degenerated into a system for excusing sin and easing the conscience without true repentance, the Puritans developed a casuistry that aimed to bind the conscience more closely to the Word, to detect the deceits of the heart, to comfort the troubled, and to direct the perplexed in the way of obedience. Such works as Perkins’s and Ames’s treatises on conscience, and Baxter’s vast Christian Directory, gathered the wisdom of Scripture and experience to answer how a Christian should pray, trade, marry, suffer, mortify sin, and discern his estate before God. This was no cold legalism but a deeply pastoral physic of the soul, treating the conscience as God’s deputy and seeking to keep it tender, instructed, and at peace through the blood of Christ. The dictionary honors Puritan casuistry as the practical flower of Reformed divinity, the application of sound doctrine to the living conscience, and a treasury for any age that would have its religion reach the heart and govern the whole of life.
webster_summary: The Reformed art of resolving cases of conscience by Scripture; the Puritans’ pastoral application of doctrine to the soul’s doubts, duties, and temptations.
webster_full: PURITAN CASUISTRY, the Reformed resolving of cases of conscience by Scripture.
Over against Roman casuistry that excused sin and eased the conscience falsely.
Bound the conscience to the Word; comforted the troubled and directed the perplexed.
Found in Perkins, Ames, and Baxter’s vast Christian Directory.
The practical flower of Reformed divinity, reaching doctrine to the heart.
scriptures: And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.

corruption_summary: Casuistry is remembered chiefly in its Roman corruption as sophistry for excusing sin; the Puritan recovery bound the conscience to the Word rather than loosing it.
corruption_paragraphs: The word casuistry has fallen into disrepute, and not without cause, for the late-medieval and Jesuit casuistry against which the Reformers reacted had in many hands become a system for finding loopholes—a sophistry that taught the conscience how to sin with less disquiet. From this abuse the modern sense of casuistry as clever evasion descends. The corruption is real, but it is a corruption of a good thing, not the thing itself.

The Puritan recovery turned casuistry to its proper end: not to ease the conscience by excusing sin, but to instruct, convict, and comfort it by the Word. Their cases of conscience sought to keep the conscience void of offence toward God and men (Acts 24:16), to resolve the doubting soul lest he sin by acting without faith (Rom 14:23), and to point the burdened to the blood of Christ that alone purges the conscience from dead works (Heb 9:14). The principle to recover is that the conscience is God’s deputy in the soul, to be bound to His Word and kept tender, never trained in evasion.
roots_summary: Puritan + casuistry (cases of conscience, Latin casus); the Reformed pastoral application of Scripture to the soul’s particular questions.
roots_lines: Casuistry — from Latin casus, a case; resolving cases of conscience.

The conscience as God’s deputy, kept tender and instructed (Act 24:16).
usage: Puritan casuistry resolved how a Christian should trade, marry, suffer, and mortify sin.
Roman casuistry excused sin; the Puritans bound the conscience to the Word instead.
Their cases of conscience are a treasury for any age that would reach the heart.

etymology: From prayer + meeting; the gathering of believers for united, corporate supplication.
biblical_def: A prayer meeting is the gathering of the saints for united, corporate supplication—the church on her knees together before the throne of grace. It rests on the promise of Christ that where two or three are gathered together in His name, there is He in the midst (Matt 18:20), and on the apostolic pattern of the church continuing with one accord in prayer (Acts 1:14), and of the gathered believers lifting up their voice to God with one accord until the place was shaken (Acts 4:24, 31). Such united prayer has stood at the headwaters of every true revival; the church has rarely been visited that was not first found pleading. The prayer meeting is not a lesser appendage to the life of the church but a chief engine of her power, the appointed means by which she lays hold of the promises, intercedes for the lost, upholds her ministers, and seeks the outpouring of the Spirit. Its decline is among the surest marks of a church grown cold, and its recovery among the first signs of returning life. The dictionary commends the prayer meeting as the gathered church’s warfare and weapon, despised by a self-confident age, but ever the secret of a praying people’s strength.
webster_summary: The gathering of believers for united corporate supplication; resting on Christ’s promise to the gathered two or three, and a chief engine of the church’s power.
webster_full: PRAYER MEETING, the gathering of believers for united supplication.
Rests on Christ’s promise to the two or three gathered in His name (Mat 18:20).
Follows the apostolic pattern of the church with one accord in prayer (Act 1:14).
Stands at the headwaters of every true revival.
Its decline marks a cold church; its recovery, returning life.
scriptures: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.

Act 4:31

corruption_summary: The prayer meeting is neglected as an optional extra or hollowed into routine; Scripture makes united prayer a chief weapon of the gathered church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is one of neglect and decay rather than of false teaching. A self-confident, activity-driven age treats the prayer meeting as an optional extra, the least-attended gathering of the week, or hollows it into a formal routine in which little is truly sought from God. This is a practical denial of the church’s dependence, a forgetting that without Christ we can do nothing, and a turning from the appointed means by which the church lays hold of her Lord’s promises.

The principle to recover is the New Testament estimate of united prayer. The early church, in danger and in growth alike, was found continuing with one accord in prayer (Acts 1:14); when they prayed, the place was shaken and they spake the word with boldness (Acts 4:31); when Peter lay in prison, prayer was made without ceasing of the church for him (Acts 12:5). The prayer meeting is not the church’s weakness but her strength, not her leisure but her warfare. A church that would see the arm of the Lord made bare must first be found, like the apostles, gathered and pleading.
roots_summary: Prayer + meeting; the gathered church’s united supplication, resting on Christ’s promise to the two or three and the apostolic pattern of one accord.
roots_lines: Prayer meeting — the gathering of believers for united supplication.

The gathered church’s weapon and warfare, not an optional extra.
